title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
hook: the brothers throw Joseph in a pit and sell him; Reuben comes back too late

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coat: a gift for the favorite son, and dreams of sheaves bowing down. Your line: favorites cost. Today we find out how much.

The brothers are far from home, pasturing the flocks, when Jacob sends Joseph to check on them. From a long way off, they see him coming. Maybe it's the coat they recognize first. They say to each other: "Behold, this dreamer cometh." Let's kill him, throw him in a pit, and say a wild animal ate him. Then we'll see what becomes of his dreams. Out in the fields, with no father watching, a family grudge turns into a plan.
screen: `THEY SEE HIM FROM FAR OFF.` → `THIS DREAMER COMETH.` → `A GRUDGE BECOMES A PLAN.`

segments.voice: Reuben, the oldest, speaks up. Don't kill him; just throw him into this pit. The Torah tells us his secret plan: come back later, pull Joseph out, and bring him home to their father. So they strip off the coat and throw Joseph in, and the text adds a detail: "the pit was empty, there was no water in it." Then, while Joseph is down there, they sit down to eat bread. A caravan passes, traders going down to Egypt. Judah has an idea: what do we gain by killing him? Let's sell him. And Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver. The text gets a little tangled here about who pulled him out and who sold him, and readers still puzzle over it. And Reuben? Somewhere else. He comes back to the pit, and it's empty. He tears his clothes: "The child is not; and as for me, whither shall I go?" The midrash has a sharp line about this. Had Reuben known that the Torah would write down that he tried to save Joseph, it says, he would have picked him up on his shoulders and carried him home to his father right then. The good intention was real. The delay cost everything. Then the brothers dip the coat in goat's blood and bring it to Jacob, and he says, "an evil beast hath devoured him." He tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and refuses to be comforted.
screen: `REUBEN: JUST THROW HIM IN THE PIT.` · `THEY SIT DOWN TO EAT BREAD.` · `SOLD FOR TWENTY PIECES OF SILVER.` · `REUBEN COMES BACK TO AN EMPTY PIT.` · then, large: `THE CHILD IS NOT.`

segments.voice: Think of one good thing you've been meaning to come back to: an apology, a call to someone who's alone, a word in someone's defense. Picture the first minute of actually doing it, then notice what's been stopping you.
Bor, Hebrew for a pit or cistern, the empty one where Joseph was thrown. Joseph is thrown into an empty pit and sold, while the brother who meant to save him is somewhere else.
Your line: don't come back too late. Reuben meant well, and found the pit empty. Day sixty-six, done.

howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers use Reuben's delay to talk about acting on a good impulse right away, echoing the saying in Pirkei Avot, if not now, when?

fork.reveal: he talks them down to the pit and plans a rescue. but he isn't there when it matters, and when he returns, the pit is empty.

original.note: Hebrew: a pit or cistern, dug to hold rainwater. this one was empty.

trapdoor: what you thought: the brothers sold Joseph, and that's the story.
what it means: one brother tried to save him and waited too long. good intentions need timing.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 37:25–36 names both Ishmaelites and Midianites, and readers still debate who sold him. the Reuben midrash is in Ruth Rabbah 5:6.

notes: Ishmaelites/Midianites ambiguity in 37:25–28 and 37:36 described as 'a little tangled'; Rashi says the brothers sold him; Rashbam says Midianites took him from the pit. Confirm framing.
Reuben midrash: Ruth Rabbah 5:6 / Leviticus Rabbah 34:8 (had Reuben known Scripture would record it, he would have carried Joseph on his shoulders). Confirm citation.
howItsDone: 'if not now, when?' is Hillel, Pirkei Avot 1:14, paraphrased without quotation marks.
